questions.q: What's the difference between Windows Authentication and SQL Server Authentication?
options: Windows Authentication uses your current Windows login; SQL Server Authentication uses a username/password stored inside SQL Server
Windows Authentication requires a password stored in SQL Server
SQL Server Authentication only works in the cloud
They are two names for the same login method
questions.explain: Windows Authentication trusts your OS login with no separate password; SQL Server Authentication is a credential SQL Server manages itself.

questions.q: What does the USE statement do?
options: Grants a user permission to a database
Sets the database context for the statements that follow it
Creates a new database connection dialog
Deletes a database
questions.explain: USE switches which database subsequent statements in the session run against.

questions.q: What is GO in a T-SQL script?
options: A batch separator recognized by SSMS, not a T-SQL statement itself
A T-SQL keyword that starts a loop
A synonym for EXECUTE
A comment marker
questions.explain: GO tells SSMS (and other T-SQL tools) where one batch ends and the next begins — the database engine itself doesn't recognize GO.

questions.q: Which function returns the name of the database your session is currently connected to?
options: DB_NAME()
SESSION_DB()
CURRENT_DATABASE
GET_DB()
questions.explain: DB_NAME() is the built-in T-SQL function for this — commonly used as SELECT DB_NAME();

questions.q: Why does every lesson script in this course open with a USE statement?
options: Because SQL Server requires USE before every SELECT
To improve query performance
So the script is unambiguous about which database it targets, regardless of what the toolbar dropdown shows
Because AdventureWorks2012 cannot be queried without it
questions.explain: Relying on the dropdown alone risks running a script against the wrong database; USE makes the target explicit in the script itself.
